why.headline: Soft, still landings let you dive and jump again in control.

claims.text: In studies of adult keepers, many saves were dives and jumps. Each one ends in a landing.
Coaches of young players ask for a held, steady landing. Jumps get longer only when landings stay steady.
Boys in their early teens trained twice weekly. After 6 weeks, long jumps were 1.1 to 6% longer. Adding jumps gave the bigger gain.
Older teen players added squats or hip lifts once a week. After 20 weeks, forward jumps were 7.5 to 13% longer.

keep_up.text: Keep training it every week to keep gains coming. In one youth study, jump gains lasted 8 weeks after training stopped. Everyone improves at their own pace.

map.plain: The big muscles at the front of your thighs
The muscles at the back of your thighs

note.text: Jump studies measured these muscles in adult athletes; none in teens.

claims.text: In adult athletes, thigh and hip muscles worked at take-off and landing.
In a youth trial, a training programme changed landing habits. Older teens improved their landings more.

limits.text: No study has tested stick landings alone in goalkeepers. The youth trials used weights and many jumps.
One youth study linked more landing errors to later knee injury. No trial shows this drill prevents injury.
